introduction-the-relativity-problem.core: Every server's clock is slightly wrong, and NTP only narrows the gap to tens or hundreds of milliseconds. If a distributed database orders events by local clocks, it can put events in the wrong order and show users impossible states.

first_principles.problem: On one machine, timestamps order events perfectly. Across three servers that disagree by 250 ms, a deposit on server A at 10:00:00.000 and a balance check on server B (clock 200 ms behind) at "09:59:59.800" look reversed, and the user sees $0 after depositing.
truths: NTP can't remove all error because network delay varies.
Ordering by wrong clocks gives wrong orderings.
derivation: Admit that **local clocks can't be trusted** for global ordering.
Name the risk: a later event gets an **earlier timestamp**.
Every NewSQL system must **bound or work around** clock error, which is what the next lessons cover.

analogy.title: Watches set by hand
analogy.story: Three friends set their watches by eye. One is 250 ms fast, one 200 ms slow. If they log events by their own watches and later merge the logs, a reply can appear to have been sent before the question.
analogy.breaks: Friends can ask each other what happened. A database must decide automatically, often in milliseconds.

example.title: The disappearing deposit
example.scenario: A deposit commits on server A at its 10:00:00.000. A balance read on server B happens after it, at B's 09:59:59.800.

steps.label: Reality
steps.detail: The read happened after the deposit.

steps.label: Timestamps
steps.detail: B's slow clock gives the read an earlier timestamp.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: Snapshot ordering hides the deposit, so the database looks wrong.

example.outcome: you see why time is a core correctness problem for distributed databases.

check.q: Why can't NTP make clocks exact?
check.a: It estimates offset from round-trip time, but one-way network delay varies and can't be measured exactly, so some error always remains.

the-gold-standard-external-consistency.core: External consistency (linearizability) means that if T1 finishes before T2 starts in real time, T1 gets a smaller timestamp. NTP's 50–500 ms error makes that impossible to guarantee without extra mechanisms.

first_principles.problem: Before choosing a solution, we need a precise goal. "Transactions appear in some order" (serializability) isn't enough for users, who expect the database to respect the order things actually happened in the real world.
truths: Users observe real-time order ("I paid, then checked").
Serializable order doesn't have to match real time.
Clock error makes real-time order ambiguous between machines.
derivation: State the rule: **T1.end < T2.start ⇒ ts(T1) < ts(T2)**.
Call it **linearizability / external consistency**, the strongest guarantee.
Note that it's **stronger than serializability**, which only needs *some* serial order.
Accept that NTP alone **can't** enforce it, so you need TrueTime or HLC + uncertainty handling.

analogy.title: A ledger with one authoritative pen
analogy.story: However many clerks are in however many cities, the ledger reads as if one pen wrote every entry in the order things truly happened. A payment made before a balance check is always written above it.
analogy.breaks: A single pen is physically one place. A global database has no single place, so it needs a clever substitute for the pen.

example.title: New York and Tokyo
example.scenario: T1 commits in New York, then the user phones a friend in Tokyo, who starts T2 and must see T1's write.

steps.label: Serializable only
steps.detail: The database may legally order T2 before T1, so the friend doesn't see the write.

steps.label: Externally consistent
steps.detail: Timestamps follow real time, so T2 sees T1.

steps.label: Mechanism
steps.detail: Needed because NY and Tokyo clocks can't be trusted to agree.

example.outcome: you can state precisely what Spanner and CockroachDB are trying to guarantee.

check.a: Serializability is equivalent to some serial order. Linearizability also requires that order to match real-time order of non-overlapping operations.

google-spanner-truetime-the-hardware-sol.core: TrueTime returns time as an interval guaranteed to contain the truth (about ±7 ms, thanks to GPS and atomic clocks). Spanner commits at the interval's upper bound and waits (about 2ε ≈ 14 ms) until that time has certainly passed.

first_principles.problem: Spanner needs external consistency across continents. Pretending clocks are exact fails silently, so it needs a way to make ordering correct despite clock error.
truths: You can't know the exact time, but you can bound the error.
After waiting out the bound, ordering is unambiguous.
derivation: Make uncertainty explicit: `TrueTime.now()` returns **[earliest, latest]**.
Keep the window tiny with **GPS + atomic clocks** in every data centre.
At commit, set **T_write = now().latest**.
**Wait** until `now().earliest > T_write` (about 2ε), then acknowledge.
Any later transaction's timestamp is necessarily greater: **guaranteed by physics**.

analogy.title: Sealing an envelope with a postmark
analogy.story: You stamp a letter with the latest time it could possibly be, then hold it until every clock in the building has passed that time before posting. Nobody can ever receive a reply stamped earlier than your letter.
analogy.breaks: Holding one letter costs a moment. Commit wait is paid on every write, so it's a hard latency floor of about 14 ms.

example.title: A write at T_write = 1000 ms

steps.label: Pick
steps.detail: Use the upper bound so no clock can think it's later than this already.

steps.label: Wait
steps.detail: About 14 ms until the lower bound has passed 1000.

steps.label: Guarantee
steps.detail: Any transaction starting now sees earliest > 1000, so it gets a larger timestamp.

example.outcome: globally correct ordering, with a fixed, predictable cost per write.

points: Hardware buys a small ε, and so a short wait.

check.q: Why can't Spanner just use NTP?
check.a: NTP error of 50–500 ms would make commit wait 100–1000 ms per write, which is unusably slow.

cockroachdb-hybrid-logical-clocks-the-so.core: CockroachDB pairs each wall-clock time with a logical counter and pushes clocks forward whenever a message with a later timestamp arrives (HLC), so cause always precedes effect. Leftover uncertainty is handled with read restarts and by shutting down nodes whose clocks drift too far.

first_principles.problem: On commodity hardware with NTP, uncertainty is 250–500 ms, so a Spanner-style commit wait would add half a second to every write. CockroachDB needs correctness without special clocks or huge waits.
truths: If B received a message from A, A's event happened first (causality).
Clocks may only ever move forward.
A bound on skew lets you detect ambiguous cases.
derivation: Timestamp = **(physical, logical)**.
On receive: physical = **max(local, incoming)**, and bump the logical counter to break ties, so time **never goes backwards** and causality is preserved.
Declare **max_offset** (500 ms default) as the tolerated skew.
On read, if a value's timestamp falls in the **uncertainty window**, **restart** the transaction at a higher timestamp.
If a node detects its clock beyond max_offset, it **shuts itself down**: availability traded for consistency.

analogy.title: Passing notes with times on them
analogy.story: Everyone writes the time on each note they pass. If you receive a note stamped later than your own watch, you move your watch forward to match. A reply can then never be stamped before the note it answers. If your watch is wildly wrong, you're asked to leave the game.
analogy.breaks: Friends can ask "which came first?". CockroachDB resolves ambiguity by restarting the transaction, which costs latency when it happens.

example.title: A message from a node whose clock is ahead
example.scenario: Node B (clock 10:00:00.100) receives a message stamped (10:00:00.300, 2).

steps.label: Jump
steps.detail: B's HLC moves to the incoming physical time.

steps.label: Tie-break
steps.detail: The logical counter becomes 3 so B's next event is strictly later.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Anything B does in response is ordered after what caused it.

example.outcome: causal order without special hardware, plus a safety net for the remaining ambiguity.

points: Clocks only move forward, so causality holds.

check.q: Why does CockroachDB shut down a node with a drifting clock?
check.a: Its timestamps could break ordering guarantees. A restarted node is far better than silent inconsistency.

comparison-truetime-vs-hlc.core: TrueTime bounds clock error with hardware and pays a fixed ~14 ms commit wait. HLC bounds it in software, pays occasional uncertainty restarts, and needs well-monitored NTP. Same problem, different trade-offs.

first_principles.problem: Both Spanner and CockroachDB promise strong consistency across machines. You need to know which mechanism fits your platform, latency budget and operations team, and what their failure modes look like.
truths: External consistency needs a bound on clock uncertainty.
Hardware bounds are tight but not portable.
Software bounds are portable but looser.
derivation: **TrueTime**: GPS/atomic clocks, ε < 7 ms, **commit wait ~14 ms** on every write, no clock-skew failure mode, Google-only.
**HLC**: NTP + logical counters, ~250–500 ms bound, **no fixed floor**, occasional **uncertainty restarts**, nodes self-terminate on drift.
Choose TrueTime for GCP, predictable latency and no restarts.
Choose HLC for multi-cloud or self-hosting, accepting restarts and **monitoring NTP** carefully.

analogy.title: Two ways to run a relay race fairly
analogy.story: One stadium installs perfect synchronised timers and makes each runner wait a fixed instant before handing off (TrueTime). Another uses ordinary watches but passes a baton with the time written on it, and re-runs a leg if the order is ever unclear (HLC).
analogy.breaks: Re-running a leg is rare and obvious. Uncertainty restarts are transparent to apps but show up as tail latency, so watch the restart metrics.

example.title: Picking for a fintech on two clouds
example.scenario: The team runs on AWS and Azure and needs serializable global transactions.

steps.label: Operate
steps.detail: chrony on every node, alert on clock offset well below max_offset.

steps.label: Watch
steps.detail: Track transaction restart rate and p99 latency for uncertainty effects.

example.outcome: a choice made on platform and operations facts, not hype.

points: Both bound uncertainty, by hardware or by software.

check.q: Which approach has a fixed per-write latency floor?
check.a: TrueTime/Spanner: commit wait of about 2ε (~14 ms) on every write.
